title: Cotton-Candy Planets: The Fluffiest Worlds Ever Found
summary: Picture a planet the size of Jupiter, but so insubstantial it could float on water — if you could find an ocean big enough. Now, imagine that same world is even less dense than the spun sugar you get at a carnival. That's exactly what an international team of astronomers has found: two “super-puff” planets that are officially fluffier than cotton candy. The planets, designated TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, orbit an F7-type dwarf star roughly 1,110 light-years away in the constellation Volans. Each is about the size of Jupiter, yet their densities are staggeringly low. TOI-791 b clocks in at 0.038 grams per cubic centimeter, while TOI-791 c is 0.047 g/cm³. For comparison, cotton candy is about 0.05 g/cm³, and Jupiter — our solar system's heavyweight — averages 1.33 g/cm³. That makes these new worlds 28 to 35 times less dense than Jupiter. Dr. [Lead author], who led the study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, noted, “Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system.” The pair is locked in a 5:3 mean-motion resonance: for every five orbits of the inner planet, the outer one completes almost exactly three. This gravitational choreography causes tiny, measurable timing variations in their transits, which allowed scientists to calculate their masses. The discovery began with citizen scientists. Volunteers in the Planet Hunters TESS project flagged the planets in 2019 and 2023 after poring over data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Researchers then combined observations from telescopes worldwide, including the ASTEP telescope at Concordia Station in Antarctica. Antarctica's months-long winter darkness was crucial: it enabled continuous monitoring of the planets' transits, which each last more than 11 hours — the longest continuous planetary transits ever fully observed from the ground. When a planet transits, or crosses in front of its star, it blocks a tiny fraction of starlight. That dip reveals the planet's size. The gravitational tugs between the two planets alter their transit timings, and by analyzing those variations, the team could estimate each planet's mass. So how do such ethereal worlds form? The leading theory is that they possess enormous, extended atmospheres rich in hydrogen and helium. These gaseous envelopes may have accumulated when the planets were much farther from their star, in the frigid outer regions of the protoplanetary disc where gas could rapidly pile onto a solid core. With only four other systems known to host multiple super-puffs, TOI-791 offers an unprecedented opportunity to test competing formation theories. Future observations, including potential studies with the James Webb Space Telescope, aim to probe the atmospheres of these bizarre planets and unravel the mystery of their origins.
why_it_matters: Discovering planets unlike any in our solar system challenges our ideas of how worlds form and hints at the wild diversity of the cosmos. Studying ‘super-puffs’ could help astronomers refine models of planetary evolution, possibly revealing where habitable worlds might arise.

background_read: Before the 1990s, astronomers didn't know if planets existed outside our solar system. Today, thanks to telescopes like NASA's TESS (launched in 2018 to scan the whole sky for alien worlds), thousands of exoplanets have been confirmed.

Most are found when they pass in front of their star, causing a tiny dip in brightness. The coldest, darkest places on Earth — like Concordia Station in Antarctica (a French-Italian research base at 3,233 meters above sea level) — allow astronomers to watch these transits continuously without the interruption of daylight.

The James Webb Space Telescope (the most powerful space observatory ever built, orbiting 1.5 million km from Earth) will soon study the atmospheres of unusual planets like these, possibly revealing what they're made of.

perspectives.description: Astronomers are thrilled because finding two super-puffs in one system is rare. This gives them a perfect laboratory to test competing theories of how planets form, using multiple planets that likely formed together.

The extreme low density is hard to explain with current models. Scientists still cannot fully account for why these planets haven't lost their puffy atmospheres, raising doubts about whether our formation theories are incomplete.

Super-puffs represent an extreme end of planetary diversity. Studying them forces astronomers to confront gaps in our knowledge of how gas giants evolve, especially in the outer regions of planetary systems.

Future telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope will measure the atmospheres directly. These observations could reveal whether super-puffs are stable worlds or doomed to evaporate over cosmic timescales.
